extracted.intended_audience: institutions and community organizations (libraries, archives, cultural organizations), scholars, librarians, archivists, and project leaders interested in Mellon Foundation Public Knowledge grants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and program priorities for applicants and potential grantees seeking Mellon Foundation Public Knowledge funding for projects that preserve, organize, and increase public access to cultural and scholarly records. Emphasizes eligible recipient types, program values, and the foundation's invitation-driven grantmaking approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program purpose — strengthen the cultural record and public access
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Public Knowledge grants support the work of the institutions and community groups that strengthen our cultural record by preserving, recording, organizing, and making knowledge accessible to the public in libraries, archives, and other settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through this work, we can build a more informed, engaged, and fair society—and ensure that vital voices and stories endure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible recipient type: Archives and libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Archives and libraries engaged in creating, preserving, and making accessible cultural and scholarly records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program supports institutions whose core work includes collection, preservation, and public access of materials; activities should directly contribute to the long-term stewardship and accessibility of cultural/scholarly records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible recipient type: Organizations addressing gaps in the historical record
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations working to address gaps in the historical record and to increase public access to knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority for efforts that identify and remedy omissions in the historical or cultural record and expand who can access or contribute to that record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible project type: Collaborative projects focused on technology and infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaborative projects focused on creating and sustaining technology and infrastructure to preserve and share knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports multi-institutional or cross-sector collaborations that build or maintain technical platforms, standards, tools, or infrastructure that enable preservation and broader sharing of cultural and scholarly materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media and methods supported: collecting across formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is alive, ever-changing. Passed on through writing, photographs, audio, and emerging forms, knowledge is pervasive—but fragile. It survives when it is collected, preserved, and shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects may involve diverse media (text, images, audio, new/digital formats) and methods of documentation, curation, and dissemination; attention to format-specific preservation and access strategies is implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program value: Treating knowledge as a public and social good
rubrics_metrics.description: “For me, public knowledge means ensuring that knowledge access and production are treated as public and social goods ... for purposes that matter to people.” — Patricia Hswe, Program Director, Public Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for projects framing knowledge access/production in terms of public benefit, community relevance, equity, and social impact rather than strictly proprietary or closed approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grantmaking approach: invitation-focused outreach and relationship-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Our staff seek out and get to know innovative leaders, scholars, librarians, archivists, and culture bearers before inviting them to submit a proposal for funding. Most Mellon grants are made through these invitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program primarily funds through staff-initiated invitations after relationship-building; prospective applicants should note that unsolicited applications may not be the primary pipeline and that cultivating relationships with program staff is important.
